evidence_chunks.text: Landfills are the primary endpoint for the disposal of PFAS-laden waste, which subsequently releases PFAS to the surrounding environments through landfill leachate. Ozone foam fractionation emerges as a promising tech - nology for PFAS removal to address the issue. This study aims to (i) assess the effectiveness of the ozone foam fractionation system to remove PFAS from landfill leachate, and (ii) quantify equilibrium PFAS adsorption onto the gas-water interface of ozone bubbles, followed by a comparison with air foam fractionation. The results show that ozone foam fractionation is effective for PFAS removal from landfill leachate, with more than 90 % long- chain PFAS removed. The identified operating conditions provide valuable insights for industrial applications, guiding the optimization of ozone flow rates (1 L/min), dosing (43 mg/L) and minimizing foamate production (4 % wettability). The equilibrium modelling reveals that the surface excess of air bubbles exceeds that of ozone bubbles by 20 – 40 % at a corresponding PFAS concentration. However, the overall removal of PFAS from landfill leachate by ozone foam fractionation remains substantial. Notably, ozone foam fractionation generates foamate volumes 2 – 4 times less, resulting in significant cost savings for the final disposal of waste products and reduced site storage requirements. 1. Foam fractionation stands out as a promising technology for removing PFAS from aqueous media (e.g. groundwater, wastewater, landfill leachate) ( Smith et al., 2022 ). Implications and future work Overall, our study indicates that differences in microbial commu - nities within the mixed liquor can influence the foaming performance observed across foam fractionation experiments. The impact should not be overlooked when optimising foam fractionation processes using mixed liquor as influent. The presence of certain foam-forming bacteria tends to increase foam formation and results in the collection of foam with a higher delivered volumetric liquid fraction. This leads to lower long-chain PFAS enrichment factors but appears not to affect PFAS concentrations reductions under similar operating conditions compared to influent without these bacteria. These findings suggest that the increased foaming performance associated with foam-forming bacteria may not meaningfully enhance integrated foam fractionation perfor - mance in aerated bioreactors, in terms of PFAS concentration reduction and enrichment. However, it is important to highlight that the typically lower foaming propensity of mixed liquor in the absence of foam- forming bacteria (and therefore resulting in thinner foam layers) may make foam harvesting challenging at full scale. Our results also showed that one of the key functional bacteria groups, namely nitrifiers, were negatively selected in the foam, providing preliminary insights that integrating foam fractionation may have minimal impact on nitrification. However, further experiments are needed to thoroughly assess the impact of foam fractionation integrating on biological wastewater treatment processes, considering the TSS mass loss observed during foam fractionation.
